title: The Judge Over the Damascus Wall
teaser: In 1401 an old judge was lowered by ropes out of besieged Damascus to meet Timur, and explained to the conqueror why conquerors fade.
story: In the winter of 1400 Timur's army came down on Syria. Aleppo fell in November. By December the tents were outside Damascus, and the Mamluk sultan Faraj, who had marched up from Cairo to stop them, hurried home instead to put down a revolt in Egypt. Among the men he left behind in the city was a judge from Cairo, born in Tunis, approaching seventy, who had spent most of his life being appointed to offices and then losing them.

The gates were shut and the guards would not open them. So Ibn Khaldun was lowered over the wall on ropes and taken to the camp. He greeted Timur in the manner of the age: 'You are the sultan of the world and the ruler of the earth.' Timur, who liked to argue, asked him to describe the Maghrib, its mountains and rivers and towns, so clearly that he might seem to see it. Ibn Khaldun spent the next few days writing the description out, and Timur had it put into Mongolian.

Then the talk turned to kings. Rule exists only through asabiyya, Ibn Khaldun told him, and the degree of rule depends on the amount of it. Of the Turks he said that none of the kings on earth was their equal in it, 'not Chosroes, nor Caesar, not Alexander, nor Nebuchadnezzar'. Timur, unimpressed by the last name, objected that Nebuchadnezzar had been merely one of the Persian generals.

Asabiyya is the word at the centre of Ibn Khaldun's thinking: group feeling, the willingness of people who believe themselves kin to stick together and fight for one another. He had set out the argument more than twenty years earlier at Qal'at ibn Salamah, a castle near what is now Frenda in Algeria, where he spent four years from 1375 writing the Muqaddimah. Cohesion of that kind, he wrote, arises by itself in tribes and small kinship groups, and it carries them to power. Power then brings cities, comfort and luxury, which quietly dissolve the thing that won it. As a rule, he concluded, no dynasty outlasts three generations, a generation being forty years. He was telling the conqueror why he had won, and, by the same argument, why what he was building would not hold.

They met repeatedly over about a month; the accounts differ on exactly how long. Ibn Khaldun gave him a Qur'an, a prayer rug and four boxes of Cairo sweets. Timur offered to buy his grey mule, and the judge replied that one like him does not sell to one like Timur, but would offer it in homage. He got his safe-conduct and went back to Egypt. Damascus was sacked anyway, the Umayyad Mosque burned in March 1401, and its craftsmen were carried off to Samarkand. Timur died in 1405 and his empire began breaking up among his descendants. Ibn Khaldun died in Cairo in March 1406.
The idea is still borrowed because it puts an awkward question to any winning side: not how strong it is, but how long its people will go on wanting to hold together.
takeaway: Asabiyya is group feeling: the willingness of people who count each other as kin to stick together and fight for one another. Ibn Khaldun argued it is what wins power, and that the comfort power brings is what dissolves it.

recall.question: In the Trobriand Islands men sailed for days to exchange shell necklaces and armbands that none of them could keep. What was that system called, and what was the point of it?
recall.answer: The kula ring: the valuables kept circulating between partners, so the lasting gain was the relationship and the prestige of having held them, not ownership.

rabbitHole.title: The arithmetic of decline
rabbitHole.intro: A theory of rise and fall, written in a castle and tested on a conqueror. What did it actually claim, how one-sided is our record of that meeting, and who uses the word now?

levels.heading: Three generations, forty years each
body: The popular version of Ibn Khaldun is a man who discovered that empires fall on a timetable. What he wrote is more specific and more modest. The Muqaddimah was not a standalone work of theory but the introduction to a long history of the Arabs and Berbers, and the cycle it describes runs through named North African dynasties.

The mechanism is generational. The first generation, he wrote in the section arguing that dynasties have a natural life span like individuals, 'retains the desert qualities, desert toughness, and desert savagery'. Settled rule then goes in for luxury and prefers tranquillity and peace; people grow used to a great number of things; the group feeling decays 'because the people who represent the group feeling have lost their energy'. Hence his rule that no dynasty lasts beyond the span of three generations, with a generation set at forty years, the figure he took for an individual's working life.

Note where the number comes from. He borrowed the hundred-and-twenty-year human lifespan from the physicians and astrologers of his day and applied it to states by analogy. It is a convention, not a measurement.

levels.heading: One side of the tent
body: Almost everything we know about the Damascus meeting comes from Ibn Khaldun's own autobiography, the Ta'rif, which he revised in Cairo afterwards. It is a flattering record for its author: he is the man the conqueror wanted to talk to, and his theory is the thing that interested him.

There is a rival account. The Syrian writer Ibn Arabshah, who loathed Timur, made Ibn Khaldun merely one member of a delegation of scholars sent out of the city. Modern accounts also disagree on the basics: Britannica says Timur asked to see him and that he spent some seven weeks in the camp; the retelling of his own narrative in Saudi Aramco World has him going out on his own initiative, lowered in a basket, and staying thirty-five days.

The scholar Josephine van den Bent, writing on the Mongols in Ibn Khaldun's work in 2016, points out how neatly the conversation served his framework. He slotted Timur's people into his categories of Mongols and Tatars, and Timur himself is made to supply the moral: their rule became formidable, he says, because they did not have luxury or comfort.

levels.heading: Asabiya with a frontier
body: The word has had a second life in English. In 'War and Peace and War' (2006) the biologist-turned-historian Peter Turchin takes asabiya from Ibn Khaldun and redefines it as the capacity of a group's members 'to stick together, to cooperate', which he treats as a quantity that rises and falls and can in principle be measured.

His addition is where it rises. Turchin argues that cohesion is forged under threat, and that the sharpest threats sit along what he calls metaethnic frontiers: the fault lines between peoples who find each other barely human. Empires, on this account, are built by groups hardened on such a frontier, and decay once the frontier has moved far away from them.

It is an adaptation rather than a restatement, and not everyone is persuaded. Reviewing the book, the economist Arnold Kling wanted a more precise definition of asabiya than he was given, and questioned whether the metaethnic boundary does the work claimed for it. The trouble with a concept that explains both rise and fall is that it is hard to catch out.

lookingGlass.heading: A cycle drawn from one region's history
body: The serious objection is to the clockwork, not the insight. Ibn Khaldun built his cycle from the Berber and Arab dynasties of the Maghrib, which did turn over quickly, and the three-generation span rests on a borrowed convention about human lifespans rather than on any count of states. Set against other histories it fails plainly: the Ottoman dynasty, already rising in his own lifetime, went on to rule for over six centuries.

His admirers have not always helped. Arnold Toynbee called the Muqaddimah the greatest work of its kind ever created by any mind in any time or place, and a long line of readers has made him the father of sociology, economics or demography in turn. Scholars including Muhsin Mahdi and Aziz al-Azmeh have pushed back, arguing that he was working within Islamic theology and philosophy and should be read on those terms rather than enlisted by whichever modern discipline wants an ancestor.
lookingGlass.verdict: Where that leaves you: take asabiyya as a sharp question about whether a group still wants to hold together, and distrust anyone, including Ibn Khaldun, who turns it into a schedule.

quiz.question: How did Ibn Khaldun get out of Damascus to meet Timur in 1401?
options: He was lowered over the city wall on ropes
He rode out through a gate opened for the sultan's envoys
He was captured in a raid and brought to the camp
He left before the siege began and waited outside
quiz.explain: The gates were shut and the guards would not open them, so he went over the wall. Timur's men then took him to the camp.

quiz.question: In Ibn Khaldun's argument, what destroys a dynasty's asabiyya?
options: The comfort and luxury that come with holding power
Disagreement among its scholars and judges
The loss of a shared language
quiz.explain: Group feeling arises in tough kinship groups and carries them to power; settled luxury then dissolves it, which is why he said no dynasty outlasts three generations.
